questions.title: Correcting a combustion measurement
questions.stem:
A burner heats water in a vessel with independently measured heat capacity 62.0 J K⁻¹. Water mass is 180.0 g; use c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Burning stops at t=5.0 min. The initial water temperature was 19.4 °C and the fuel mass loss is 0.620 g. Fuel molar mass is 60.1 g mol⁻¹.

| Cooling time / min | 5.5 | 6.0 | 6.5 | 7.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Temperature / °C | 32.5 | 32.3 | 32.1 | 31.9 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the cooling trend to estimate the temperature at shutdown and the corrected temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy absorbed by water and vessel, and the experimental molar enthalpy of combustion.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A reference value for the same fuel and product states is −2020 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage of reference energy recovered and explain one chemical and one physical source of deficit.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suppose fuel evaporates unburnt during weighing. Predict its effect and propose a paired control to estimate its magnitude.

steps.text: Cooling slope is −0.4 K min⁻¹.
At 5.0 min the extrapolated temperature is 32.7 °C.
Corrected rise is 13.3 K.
Combined heat capacity=180.0×4.18+62.0=814.4 J K⁻¹.
ΔHexp≈−1.05×10³ kJ mol⁻¹.
Incomplete combustion to CO or soot releases less energy per mole of fuel.
Heat escapes to the air or unaccounted apparatus while the burner runs, which extrapolation after shutdown cannot fully restore.
The measured mass loss includes unburnt fuel, so moles burned are overestimated.
The apparent combustion enthalpy then has too small a magnitude.
Weigh an identical unlit burner over the same handling interval and conditions to estimate evaporation; accept a suitable capped-burner comparison with limitations.

questions.title: Pressure tracking in a sealed cell
questions.stem:
Initially a rigid 1.000 dm³ vessel contains only N₂O₄(g) at 300.0 K and 100.0 kPa. It is held at 300.0 K as N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) approaches equilibrium. Treat gases as ideal, with R=8.31 kPa dm³ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The final pressure is 130.0 kPa.

| t / s | 0 | 20 | 40 | 80 | 160 | 240 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| p / kPa | 100 | 112 | 120 | 127 | 130 | 130 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the initial amount of N₂O₄ and the fraction that dissociates.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate both equilibrium concentrations and Kc using concentrations in mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Estimate the mean formation rate of NO₂ from 20 to 80 s. Explain the factor linking increase in total moles to moles of NO₂ formed.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student interprets a rising pressure as sufficient proof of dissociation. Give a competing explanation and an experimental check. Explain why a plateau alone does not prove dynamic equilibrium.

steps.text: For dissociated fraction α, total moles are n₀(1+α), and pressure is proportional to total moles.
Kc=[NO₂]²/[N₂O₄]=0.0206 using the stated concentration convention.
One mole dissociated increases total moles by one but forms two moles NO₂; Δn(NO₂)=0.0120 mol.
Heating a sealed fixed amount of gas can also raise its pressure.
Monitor the gas temperature independently in a thermostatted bath and test the vessel for leaks.
A flat reading shows constant pressure within resolution; ongoing equal forward and reverse rates require chemical evidence or consistency with reversible changes.

questions.title: A cell under load
questions.stem:
A Zn/Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺/Cu cell is measured at 298 K. Standard reduction potentials are −0.76 V and +0.34 V respectively. Both initial solutions are taken as standard for the theoretical calculation. Use F=96,500 C mol⁻¹. The meter’s absolute uncertainty is ±0.01 V for each reading.

| Condition | Fresh, open circuit | Connected to resistor | Open circuit after disconnecting |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Voltage / V | 1.09 | 0.93 | 1.08 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the net ionic reaction and calculate the standard potential and Gibbs energy change per mole of Zn.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare the two open-circuit readings with each other using maximum absolute uncertainties. Is the decline resolved?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the loaded voltage is unsuitable for a direct calculation of standard Gibbs energy and identify the direction of electron flow through the resistor.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A technician replaces the salt bridge with a dry insulating strip. Explain the resulting behaviour and propose a control that tests the bridge rather than the electrodes.

steps.text: Zn(s)+Cu²⁺(aq)→Zn²⁺(aq)+Cu(s).
The measured fall is 0.01 V.
Maximum uncertainty in the difference is 0.01+0.01=0.02 V.
Zero difference is possible within this range, so a decline is not resolved.
A current produces internal voltage losses/polarization, so the terminal voltage under load is not the reversible standard emf.
Electrons flow from Zn, the oxidation electrode, toward Cu.
Charge imbalance builds up in the half-cells without ion migration.
Sustained external electron flow ceases even if a brief transient is seen.
Restore the original conducting salt bridge with electrodes and solutions unchanged and check whether the normal current/voltage behaviour returns.

questions.answerSummary: Restore the original conducting salt bridge with electrodes and solutions unchanged and check whether the normal current/voltage behaviour returns.
